## AI tutor {#sec-tutor-welcome}

You're not alone with this book. Every chapter of this part links to the same
AI tutor, a chat that knows what the course has taught you so far. Ask it
whenever an explanation doesn't click, and it helps you with the commands you
already have instead of jumping ahead.

{{< tutor tutor-introduction >}}

## Welcome to Creative Coding {#sec-welcome}

Welcome to this course! Over the next months you'll learn how to program a
computer, and you'll do it in a creative way. Instead of only printing text on
a black screen, you'll draw shapes, build animations, and create small
interactive artworks and games. That's why the course is called *Creative
Coding*: you learn programming by making things you can see, change, and show
to your friends.

You don't need any programming experience to start. The course begins at zero
and builds up step by step. If you can use a computer and you're curious, you
have everything you need.

## The tools you'll use {#sec-tools}

In this course you'll work with two tools: a programming language called
**TypeScript** and a graphics library called **p5.js**. Together they let you
write real, professional-style code and see the results on screen right away.

### TypeScript, the language {#sec-typescript}

TypeScript is one of the most popular programming languages in the world.
Many well-known websites and apps are built with it, and professional
developers use it every day. So you're not learning a toy language made only
for classrooms: the skills you pick up here are the same skills used in real
software teams.

At the same time, TypeScript is friendly to beginners. It watches your code
while you type and warns you about many mistakes before you even run the
program. Think of it as a language with a built-in spell checker for code.

### p5.js, the graphics library {#sec-p5js}

p5.js is a **library** for creating interactive graphics and animations. A
library is a collection of ready-made code that you can use in your own
programs. Instead of writing hundreds of lines yourself just to draw a circle,
you call one short command from the library and the circle appears. Libraries
let you build on the work of other programmers, which is how almost all
software is made.

p5.js was created for students and artists. It's designed so that your very
first program can be just a few lines that draw something on screen. From
there you can build up: shapes become patterns, patterns become animations,
and animations become games and interactive art.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Simple start, no limits
With p5.js you can draw your first circle in minutes, but people also use it
for serious generative art and data visualizations. You won't outgrow it
during this course.
:::

## Why learn to code when AI writes code? {#sec-why-code}

Maybe you're thinking: "AI tools can write code now. Why should I learn it
myself?" That's a fair question, and it deserves an honest answer. Here are
four reasons.

### Programming is more than typing code {#sec-problem-solving}

When you program, the typing is the smallest part. The real work is thinking:
you take a big, fuzzy problem, break it into small clear steps, and put those
steps in a logical order. You also make creative decisions, because there is
almost never just one way to solve a problem. These skills, breaking problems
down, thinking logically, and finding creative solutions, help you far beyond
programming: in school, in any job, and whenever you face something
complicated.

### AI is like a genie in a lamp {#sec-genie}

You may know the old story of the genie in the lamp: a magical being appears
and grants your wishes. But there's a catch. The genie gives you exactly what
you *say*, not what you *mean*. Wish carelessly and you get something you
didn't want at all.

AI works the same way. It will happily produce code for you, but the result is
only as good as your wish. To get useful code, you need to know what is
possible, what to ask for, and how to judge what you get back. Learning to
program by hand teaches you exactly that. You learn what a computer can do,
how software is built, and what a good solution looks like. In short: you
learn what to wish for.

### Someone has to fix the last few percent {#sec-last-percent}

AI makes mistakes. It writes code that looks correct but sometimes isn't, and
it can get stuck on the tricky final details of a program. Professionals are
the people who spot those mistakes and fix the last few percent that the AI
can't get right. You can only do that if you understand the code yourself.
The better you understand programming, the more powerful AI becomes as your
assistant instead of your replacement.

### Programming is fun {#sec-fun}

Last but definitely not least: programming is fun. There's a special feeling
when you imagine something, write the code for it, and watch the computer
bring it to life exactly the way you pictured it (or in a surprising way
that's even better). In this course that feeling comes quickly, because your
programs draw, move, and react from the very first lessons.

## A coding assistant from your teacher {#sec-coding-assistant}

Besides the tutor, this course has a second AI, and your teacher decides when
you get it. It's a **coding assistant**, and it differs from the tutor in one
important way. The tutor explains and asks questions, while the coding
assistant writes real code together with you.

Access works with a **Coding Activity Code**, a short code your teacher hands
out for a homework assignment, a workshop day at school, or a project week.
The code costs you nothing, and it works only for the time your teacher set,
so it stops working once that time is over.

### Why not just any AI from the internet {#sec-coding-assistant-why}

The coding assistant knows this course. The coding rules of this book are
built into it, so it writes the kind of code you can read, explain, and defend
in class, and it stays with the commands you've already learned instead of
jumping ahead.

A general AI on the internet knows nothing about your course. It writes code
the way it would for a professional, full of things nobody has shown you yet.
Code like that might run, but you can't explain it, and you can't repair it
when it breaks. You're the one who hands the program in, so you're the one who
has to understand every line of it.

### Where the coding assistant works {#sec-coding-assistant-where}

In the first parts of this course you write your programs in a web playground,
an editor that runs in your browser (@sec-playground). With a Coding Activity
Code, the coding assistant is there with you. It reads your program, explains
it, and shows you new code in the chat. Typing that code into your program
stays your job, and that's exactly how it ends up in your head.

Later in the course you'll move to Visual Studio Code on your own computer.
There you enter a Coding Activity Code in a free, open source coding agent
such as [pi.dev](https://pi.dev) or [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai), and the
assistant works directly with the files of your project. Your teacher tells
you which agent your class uses and how to set it up.
